description: Test your knowledge of PA NS1 | Nervous System & Eye — Meningitis classification, pathogenesis, and clinical correlations for MBBS students.

cards.text: Define meningitis and explain the three main classifications based on CSF findings.
cards.answer: Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges (arachnoid + pia). It is classified as: (1) Purulent/pyogenic (bacterial) — neutrophilic exudate, turbid CSF; (2) Aseptic (viral) — lymphocytic exudate, clear CSF; (3) Chronic (tubercular/fungal) — lymphocytic/mixed exudate with basal predominance.

tip.tip: Remember: Purulent = Pus (turbid), Aseptic = clear, Chronic = basal

cards.text: Name the three main pathogenetic routes by which organisms reach the meninges.
cards.answer: (1) Haematogenous (most common) — organism enters blood, seeds meninges from bacteraemia/viraemia; (2) Direct extension — from adjacent foci (sinusitis, otitis media, skull fracture); (3) Retrograde neuronal transport — viral pathogens travel along axons (e.g., HSV, rabies).

cards.text: Which bacteria cause meningitis in neonates (0–4 weeks) and why?
cards.answer: E. coli (K1 capsule), Group B Streptococcus (S. agalactiae), and Listeria monocytogenes. These organisms are acquired maternally during delivery or early postnatal exposure; immature immune system cannot contain them.

tip.tip: EGL: E. coli, Group B Strep, Listeria (neonatal trio)

cards.text: Which organism is the most common cause of meningitis in children aged 5–30 years, and what is its hallmark clinical sign?
cards.answer: Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus) is most common in children and young adults. Hallmark sign is petechial/purpuric rash; fulminant cases present with Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome (bilateral adrenal haemorrhage causing adrenal failure).

cards.text: Compare the most common meningitis pathogen in adults (>30 years) vs elderly/immunocompromised patients.
cards.answer: Adults (>30 years): Streptococcus pneumoniae is most common and most lethal form with highest mortality and neurological sequelae. Elderly/immunocompromised: Listeria monocytogenes and Gram-negative rods become more prevalent.

cards.text: What structural feature do meningitis-causing bacteria share, and how does it facilitate CNS invasion?
cards.answer: All meningitis-causing bacteria possess a polysaccharide capsule (e.g., S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis, E. coli K1). The capsule resists phagocytosis, allowing persistence in blood and penetration of the blood–brain barrier to seed the meninges.

tip.tip: Capsule = "stealth coat" — protects from immune system

cards.text: Describe the pathogenic cascade from bacterial CNS entry to raised intracranial pressure in meningitis.
cards.answer: Bacteria enter subarachnoid space → bacterial products activate pattern-recognition receptors (TLRs) on microglia/macrophages → pro-inflammatory cytokine storm (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6) → increased BBB permeability → neutrophil influx → purulent exudate → exudate obstructs CSF flow → communicating hydrocephalus and raised ICP.

tip.tip: Bacteria → Cytokines → Exudate → Obstruction → Raised ICP

cards.text: What are the main vascular and neuronal complications of acute bacterial meningitis?
cards.answer: Vasculitis of meningeal and cortical vessels can lead to infarction (stroke). Bacterial toxins and inflammatory mediators cause direct neuronal injury. Combined with raised ICP and compromised cerebral perfusion, these result in seizures, loss of consciousness, and permanent neurological sequelae (deafness, cognitive impairment).

tip.tip: Vasculitis → Stroke; Toxins → Neuronal death; ICP ↑ → Brain damage
